C45233.observed: What was checked: what the "Bin Locations" window lists, and what its "Auto" button does when there is more than one bin to spread across. What happened: the window names the part and lists one row per bin under BIN NAME, QUANTITY IN STOCK and AMOUNT - General Storage (marked Default) 8, A1A 5, A1B 3, A1C 2 - each with a box for how many to take from it, and it offers Auto, Cancel and Apply. A quantity of 15 was asked for, which no single bin can supply. Before Auto the whole 15 sat on the default bin. Pressing Auto spread it sensibly: it filled the default bin first to its full 8, then took 5 from the next largest, A1A, and the remainder from the next - reaching 15 without asking any bin for more than it holds.

C45234.observed: What was checked: whether Apply carries a genuine multi-bin split back to the row, and what the quantity ends up as. What happened: with 15 spread across three bins, Apply closed the window and the row came back with a quantity of 15 - the total of the three amounts. The window states this before you press it: "Allocated 15 — the row quantity will be set to 15." So the quantity and the bins it is drawn from always agree.

C45225.observed: What was checked: how the chip under the row is labelled, for a single bin and for a split. What happened, both ways. Where the whole quantity comes from one bin the chip carries that bin's name - "General Storage", or "A1A" once a different bin was chosen by hand. Where the quantity is spread, the chip reads "3 bins" instead of naming any one of them - so the technician can see at a glance that the part is coming from more than one place, and can open the chip for the detail.

C45243.observed: What was checked: whether the "takes this bin negative" warning wrongly appears on a split, where it would be meaningless. What happened: asking for 15 from a part whose default bin holds only 8 did show the warning - "Only 8 here. Pulling 15 takes this bin negative." - while the whole 15 sat on that one bin. After the same 15 was split across three bins, the warning was gone: no bin was being asked for more than it holds, so there was nothing to warn about. The warning belongs to single-bin allocations only, exactly as the case requires.
